 Amid SNAP cuts, Lumbee food sovereignty fills the gap
 Native Americans report higher rates of food-related diseases and rely more heavily on federal nutritional programs while food sovereignty works to fill the gaps amid social service reductions. 
 Kate Bumgarner , Escritora 
 • 
 November 16, 2026 
 The collard sandwich, a North Carolina Lumbee Tribe staple, is sold by the Snak Shak in Robeson County. Photo and caption information courtesy of Elizabeth Shestak/ourstate.com. 
 Native food sovereignty — the ability of an Indigenous community to control the production, cultivation and distribution of food — runs much deeper than solely fighting hunger.  
 Native cuisine can be divided into pre- and post-contact diets, according to the National Indian Council on Aging, Inc. There are traditional Native foods, made with ingredients that relied on the terrain of the land before European contact, and post-contact foods, which are foods that Native communities have adapted and integrated into their diets and culture.  
 Native American people in North Carolina have historically relied on wild nuts, foraged produce, fish and game, as well as farmed maize, beans and squash. 
 An example of post-contact cultural food is the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina’s collard sandwich. The sandwich is two slices of cornbread — originating from the Americas — filled with the non-Indigenous collard greens melted into pork fat and topped with fatback. It’s often served with a side of chow-chow, a pickled vegetable relish.  
 Joy Hunt is a Lumbee dietitian specializing in Native foodways and chronic, diet-related conditions like diabetes and hypertension. Native Americans self-report higher rates of these diseases than other ethnic groups, according to a 2012 review by Purdue University researchers. Many of Hunt’s patients are Lumbee citizens, including elders. 
 “That is a part of food as medicine, to make sure that you are connecting with the foods that remind you of home, that bring you back to your culture, that bring you back to that identity, that kind of root you further into yourself and who you are,” Hunt said.  
 Native Americans are much more likely to rely on benefits such as SNAP, food banks and other assistance programs, according to the Center for Financial Security at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. These programs cannot always provide the nutrient-rich foods Native communities have relied on for generations. 
 “These programs, unfortunately, do benefit my patients in the sense that they give them access to food, but it’s not food that is culturally relevant, and it’s not always food that’s good for the disease state that they have,” Hunt said.  
 With recent SNAP cuts, many of Hunt’s patients face a greater fear: no food at all.  
 New work requirements for SNAP eligibility under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act have tightened the pool of people who can receive nutritional assistance in North Carolina. Further eligibility restrictions loom as the U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed on Nov. 10 to eliminate broad-based categorical eligibility for the program. 
 Hunt said that in times of need, the Lumbee Tribe has provided food boxes to her patients, which gave them access to fresh, healthy food.  
 Larry Edwards, community development organizer for Triangle Native American Society, explained that providing for the community is important to the Lumbee Tribe.  
 “I remember myself, you know, as a kid, it wasn’t just putting up food. Say if we were doing sweet corn, that wasn’t just for us and our family. But it was Miss Ethel that was down the street because her husband just passed, so we put them up for her,” Edwards said.  
 Edwards said that it is common for members of the tribe to maintain a self-sustaining system, such as planting a garden.  
 “Food sovereignty for us was not just the ownership of food and us being able to provide for ourselves and our families, but it was being able to provide for our communities,” Edwards said. 
 The Lumbee Tribe sees food as medicine, not just for the body, but for the community, Edwards said.  
 Lumbee chef Christina Strickland Theodorou approaches food sovereignty with an emphasis on reclamation.  
 “Indigenous food sovereignty really is about telling the truth of the Americas, telling the truth that soul food — Southern food is Indigenous food, right? Cooking with cornmeal, that’s Indigenous. Barbecue, that’s Indigenous. Chow-chow, that’s an Indigenous word,” Strickland Theodoro said.  
 Strickland Theodorou said that without the food of pre-colonial America, the global culinary scene could not exist. She used tomatoes in Italian food as an example.  
 “It’s speaking the truth and claiming our actual food cultural heritage. So then our children would be proud to eat the things that come from their grandparents’ farms and gardens,” Strickland Theodorou said.  
 Strickland Theodorou said food sovereignty is something that everyone should have a right to.  
 “It is health, it’s sustenance, it’s sustainability, it’s relationship building. Whenever you go and visit someone’s house, and the first thing that they ask, other than to sit, ‘Would you like something to drink? Would you like something to eat?’ That’s how you show love to one another,” Edwards said.
